analysis.one_liner: Strips the FCC's authority to enforce net neutrality rules on broadband providers.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Mike Lee with 11 Republican cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or a vote, leaving the 2015 net neutrality rules in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the FCC's 2015 rule that reclassified broadband internet as a 'telecommunications service,' which is the legal basis for net neutrality — the requirement that internet providers treat all web traffic equally. It would also ban the FCC from issuing the same rule again unless Congress passes a new law specifically authorizing it. In practice, broadband companies like cable and phone firms could block, slow down, or charge websites extra for faster delivery, with no federal regulator empowered to stop them. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband internet providers — large cable and telephone companies — gain the most. The 2015 rule gave the FCC power to police how these companies handle internet traffic, including bans on blocking websites, slowing traffic, and selling 'fast lanes' to websites that pay extra. Nullifying the rule and barring the FCC from reissuing it would free these companies from those obligations and from the threat of future reclassification.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the FCC's February 26, 2015 rule reclassifying broadband internet access as a telecommunications service 'shall have no force or effect.'
It prohibits the FCC from reissuing that rule in substantially the same form, or issuing a substantially similar new rule, unless Congress specifically authorizes it by a law enacted after this bill.
That would end the FCC's common-carrier authority over broadband, the legal foundation for enforcing net neutrality rules against internet providers.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users, small websites, and startups bear the cost. Without net neutrality rules, broadband companies could charge websites for priority delivery, favor their own video and content services over rivals, and throttle or block services they dislike — costs that would flow to consumers through higher prices, fewer choices, and slower access to sites that can't or won't pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the only federal rules requiring broadband providers to treat all internet traffic equally, leaving consumers without enforceable protections against blocking, throttling, or paid prioritization of content.
Because it also bars the FCC from reissuing a substantially similar rule on its own, the protections would not come back unless Congress passed a new law specifically authorizing them.

Supporters argued the 2015 rules treated lightly-regulated internet service like a 1930s utility and discouraged network investment; the bill reflected that view, but it offered no substitute consumer protections in their place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to a handful of large broadband providers, which would gain freedom from traffic-handling rules and from the possibility of future regulation. The costs fall on the public: everyone who uses the internet would lose the guarantee that their provider delivers all websites equally. Supporters' argument that regulation deters infrastructure investment was the strongest good-faith case for the bill, but it did not include replacement safeguards, so the bill amounted to a one-sided removal of consumer protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on May 1, 2017, for himself and eight other Republican senators.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
Eleven Republican senators signed on as cosponsors.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary internet users and online businesses kept the 2015 net neutrality rules in effect, because the bill died in committee without a vote. Broadband providers remained subject to the FCC's traffic-handling rules, at least through this legislative channel.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet users kept net neutrality rules

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the FCC's 2015 broadband reclassification rule and bar the FCC from reissuing it.

for.name: 11 of 52 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Cornyn, Cotton, Cruz, Johnson, Paul, Tillis, Sasse, and Inhofe among the original nine.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill (chaired by Sen. John Thune)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters were Republicans — the sponsor plus 11 cosponsors — and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill would free them from common-carrier rules that ban blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization, letting them charge websites for faster delivery and favor their own content services. Their gain comes directly at the expense of internet users' equal access.

industries.industry: Internet content and edge companies, startups, and small websites
industries.note: Websites and online services would have to pay broadband providers for priority delivery or risk being slowed, a cost that hits startups and small sites hardest and gets passed to consumers.
